titles: Germany Reunited 36 Years Ago. Its Money Map Didn't
Borders That Vanished Still Decide Who's Rich
A Coastline From the Age of Dinosaurs Still Shapes Who's Poor
thumbnails: 1: Germany's 2025 GDP-per-person map (our engine, AK VGRdL data) with the vanished East–West border glowing on the colour edge: "GONE 1990" + "STILL THERE"
2: The Black Belt crescent from space (NASA Earth Observatory, PD): "DINOSAUR COAST" + "STILL POOR"
3: Rome's Limes glowing across a map of Germany: "ROME'S LINE" + "STILL GLOWS"
hook: Germany erased its East–West border in 1990, yet in 2025 not one of the five eastern states produced as much per person as the poorest western state. Poland's century-old partition lines, the Habsburg border, Rome's frontier and even a coastline from the age of dinosaurs still show up in today's money — and some don't. Which ghost borders fade, which ones stay, and why? Explained with maps, charts and real research. No background needed. Not financial advice.
credits: Map data: Natural Earth admin-1, coastlines, relief and rivers (public domain) via world-atlas; US counties: us-atlas (ISC) from US Census Bureau data (public domain). Historic border lines (1914 borders, Roman Limes) are our own approximate tracings from public-domain maps.

Data: AK VGR der Länder 2026 (GDP per person by state); Destatis (wages 1991–2025); IW / ifo via press reports; University of Alabama Education Policy Center (2025); US Census ACS via USAFacts; US Census 1860 via JCSSR 2023; Encyclopedia of Alabama. Ratios marked 'our arithmetic' are calculated from these sources.

Research: Grosfeld & Zhuravskaya, Journal of Comparative Economics 2015 and working paper 2023; Becker, Boeckh, Hainz & Woessmann, Economic Journal 2016 (IZA DP 5584); Wahl, Journal of Economic Growth 2017 (Hohenheim DP 08-2015); NASA Earth Observatory 'Black Belt Prairie' (2018).
